styles.how: A single fermentation in a pressure tank, stopped early by chilling so sugar and some bubbles remain (Asti method).
styles.taste: Grapes, peach, orange blossom; sweet, light, about 5–7.5% abv.

styles.name: Noble rot wines
styles.summary: Luscious wines from grapes concentrated by Botrytis cinerea.
styles.how: In misty autumn mornings and sunny afternoons, botrytis pierces the skins; water evaporates and sugar, acid and flavor concentrate. Grapes are picked berry by berry over several passes.
styles.taste: Honey, apricot, marmalade, ginger and saffron; very sweet yet balanced by acidity.

styles.name: Icewine
styles.summary: Pressed from grapes frozen on the vine.
styles.how: Grapes hang into winter and freeze at about −8 °C or below. Pressed while frozen, only a few drops of concentrated sugary juice emerge.
styles.taste: Pure, intense fruit (peach, lychee, citrus) with vivid acidity; no botrytis notes.

styles.name: Dried-grape wines
styles.summary: Grapes dried after harvest to concentrate sugar.
styles.how: Bunches dry on mats, racks or in lofts for weeks or months (appassimento or passito) before pressing.
styles.taste: Raisin, fig, dried cherry, nuts; sweet, or dry and powerful if fully fermented (Amarone).

styles.name: Ruby, Reserve & Vintage Port
styles.summary: Deep, sweet, fruit-driven fortified reds from the Douro.
styles.how: Fortified mid-fermentation, then aged in large vessels or bottle to preserve fruit. Vintage Port spends about two years in wood, then ages for decades in bottle.
styles.taste: Blackberry, black cherry, chocolate, spice; sweet, tannic, about 20% abv.

styles.name: Tawny Port
styles.summary: Port aged in small casks for nutty, oxidative character.
styles.how: Long oxidative ageing in small barrels turns the wine tawny. Indications of age (10, 20, 30, 40 years) are blends showing an average character.
styles.taste: Walnut, toffee, caramel, dried fig and orange peel.

styles.name: Fino & Manzanilla
styles.summary: Bone-dry, pale Sherries aged under a blanket of flor yeast.
styles.how: Fortified to about 15% so flor can grow. The flor protects the wine from oxygen and adds bread dough and almond notes.
styles.taste: Almond, bread dough, chamomile, saline; dry and tangy. Serve chilled.

styles.name: Oloroso & sweet Sherries
styles.summary: Sherries aged in contact with oxygen; dry unless sweetened.
styles.how: Fortified to about 17%, which prevents flor. Oxidative ageing in a solera darkens the wine and builds nutty flavors. Sweet styles use PX or Moscatel, or are blended (Cream).
styles.taste: Walnut, toffee, leather, dried fruit; PX is raisiny and syrupy.

styles.name: Madeira
styles.summary: Heated, oxidized fortified wine from a Portuguese island; nearly indestructible.
styles.how: Fortified, then heated (estufagem in tanks, or canteiro in warm lofts for years). Styles run from dry Sercial to rich Malmsey.
styles.taste: Caramel, toffee, walnut, orange peel; tangy acidity whatever the sweetness.

styles.name: Vins doux naturels
styles.summary: Southern French sweet wines fortified during fermentation.
styles.how: Grape spirit added early, like Port, keeping natural grape sugar. Made from Muscat (fresh, floral) or Grenache (Banyuls, Maury: red, sometimes oxidative).
styles.taste: Muscat: orange blossom, grape, peach. Grenache: red fruit, chocolate, coffee.

steps.title: Sugar
steps.text: Ripe grapes are full of sugar (glucose and fructose).

steps.title: Yeast
steps.text: Yeast, natural or added, feeds on the sugar.

steps.title: Alcohol
steps.text: Sugar becomes **alcohol** and **carbon dioxide**, plus heat and flavor compounds.

steps.title: CO₂
steps.text: Usually escapes. Trap it and you get bubbles.

steps.title: Harvest
steps.text: Grapes picked at the right balance of sugar and acid, often in the cool of morning.

steps.title: Crush & press
steps.text: Juice is separated from skins **before** fermentation, so the wine stays pale.

steps.title: Cool fermentation
steps.text: Usually 12–22 °C in stainless steel to keep fresh fruit aromas.

steps.title: Optional maturation
steps.text: On lees, in oak, or with malolactic conversion for richer styles.

steps.title: Clarify & bottle
steps.text: Fined, filtered, stabilized and bottled.

steps.title: Harvest
steps.text: Black grapes picked when skins and seeds are ripe.

steps.title: Crush
steps.text: Grapes are lightly crushed; juice stays **with the skins**.

steps.title: Warm fermentation
steps.text: 20–32 °C extracts color and tannin. The cap of skins is punched down or pumped over.

steps.title: Maceration
steps.text: Skins may stay in after fermentation to extract more.

steps.title: Press
steps.text: The new wine is drained and the skins pressed.

steps.title: Maturation
steps.text: Malolactic conversion, then months or years in tank or oak before bottling.

steps.title: Black grapes
steps.text: Rosé is made from black grapes.

steps.title: Short skin contact
steps.text: A few hours to a couple of days, just enough for a pink color.

steps.title: Run off or press
steps.text: Juice is separated from the skins, or grapes are pressed directly.

steps.title: Ferment like a white
steps.text: Cool temperatures keep fresh red-fruit aromas.

steps.title: Base wine
steps.text: A high-acid, still, dry wine, often a blend.

steps.title: Liqueur de tirage
steps.text: Wine, sugar and yeast are added and the bottle is sealed with a crown cap.

steps.title: Second fermentation
steps.text: In the bottle. The CO₂ is trapped and dissolves: the wine becomes sparkling.

steps.title: Ageing on lees
steps.text: Months to years in contact with dead yeast: biscuit, bread and brioche aromas (autolysis).

steps.title: Riddling
steps.text: Bottles are turned and tilted until the yeast collects in the neck.

steps.title: Disgorgement
steps.text: The neck is frozen and the plug of yeast shoots out.

steps.title: Dosage
steps.text: A little wine and sugar sets the sweetness, from Brut Nature to Doux.

steps.title: Base wine
steps.text: Often from aromatic grapes such as Glera.

steps.title: Second fermentation in tank
steps.text: In a large sealed pressure tank, not in bottle.

steps.title: Filter & bottle
steps.text: Filtered and bottled under pressure, ready to drink.

steps.title: Result
steps.text: Fresh, fruity and floral, with little or no yeasty character. Prosecco is the best-known example.

steps.title: Whole bunches
steps.text: Uncrushed bunches go into a vessel filled with carbon dioxide.

steps.title: Fermentation inside the berry
steps.text: Without oxygen, an enzyme starts converting sugar to alcohol inside each grape.

steps.title: Press
steps.text: Berries burst or are pressed; fermentation finishes as normal.

steps.title: Result
steps.text: Deep color, soft tannins, and aromas of banana, kirsch and bubblegum: classic Beaujolais Nouveau.

steps.title: Stop the fermentation
steps.text: Chill, filter or add alcohol (fortification) while sugar remains.

steps.title: Late harvest
steps.text: Leave grapes on the vine to ripen and shrivel: Spätlese, Vendanges Tardives.

steps.title: Noble rot
steps.text: *Botrytis cinerea* pierces the skins and concentrates sugar and acid: Sauternes, Tokaji, Beerenauslese.

steps.title: Frozen grapes
steps.text: Grapes freeze on the vine and are pressed frozen, leaving concentrated juice: Icewine, Eiswein.

steps.title: Dried grapes
steps.text: Grapes are dried after picking (passito): Recioto, Vin Santo, Pedro Ximénez.

steps.title: Sweet reserve
steps.text: Unfermented grape juice blended back into dry wine.

steps.title: Douro grapes
steps.text: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and other native black grapes.

steps.title: Intense extraction
steps.text: Traditionally foot-trodden in stone lagares; now often robotic treaders.

steps.title: Fortify early
steps.text: Halfway through fermentation, grape spirit (77% abv) is added. Yeast dies and sugar remains.

steps.title: Mature
steps.text: **Ruby** styles in large vessels to keep fruit; **tawny** styles in small casks for oxidative, nutty character.

steps.title: Palomino base wine
steps.text: A neutral, dry white from the chalky albariza soils around Jerez.

steps.title: Fortification
steps.text: To 15–15.5% for biological ageing (fino) or 17% for oxidative ageing (oloroso).

steps.title: Flor or oxygen
steps.text: **Flor**, a layer of yeast, protects Fino and Manzanilla from oxygen. Without flor, Oloroso oxidizes and darkens.

steps.title: Solera
steps.text: Fractional blending across rows of barrels keeps the style consistent year after year.

steps.title: Look
steps.text: Clarity, intensity and color, against a white background.

steps.title: Smell
steps.text: Swirl, then sniff. Intensity first, then the aroma families.

steps.title: Taste
steps.text: Sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body, flavors and the length of the finish.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.text: Quality and readiness: is it balanced, intense, complex and long?

steps.title: New barrels
steps.text: Add flavor: vanilla, toast, clove, coconut, smoke.

steps.title: Slow oxygen
steps.text: Tiny amounts of oxygen through the staves soften tannin and deepen color.

steps.title: Old barrels
steps.text: Add little flavor but still allow gentle oxygen exposure.

steps.title: Cheaper options
steps.text: Oak chips or staves in a tank add oak flavors quickly, without the oxygen effect.

items.name: Clarity
items.tip: Most wines are clear. Haze can mean a fault, or an unfiltered natural wine.

items.name: Intensity
items.tip: Look down through the glass at the core. Can you see the stem through a red?

items.name: Color
items.tip: For whites. Reds run **purple → ruby → garnet → tawny → brown**; rosés are **pink, salmon, orange**.

items.name: Condition
items.tip: Musty, wet-cardboard notes suggest cork taint (TCA). Flat bruised-apple notes suggest oxidation.

items.name: Intensity
items.tip: Do the aromas leap out, or do you have to search for them?

items.name: Development
items.tip: Only fresh fruit means youthful. Tertiary notes (leather, honey, nuts) mean it is developing.

items.name: Characteristics
items.tip: Work through the aroma families: fruit, floral, herbal, spice, then winemaking and ageing notes.

items.name: Sweetness
items.tip: Feel it on the tip of the tongue. Ripe fruit flavors can feel sweet in a dry wine, so be careful.

items.name: Acidity
items.tip: How much does your mouth water? How sharp is it on the sides of the tongue?

items.name: Tannin
items.tip: The drying, gripping feeling on gums and teeth. Note its texture too: fine, ripe, coarse or green.

items.name: Alcohol
items.tip: A warming feeling at the back of the throat. Below 11% is low; 14% and above is high.

items.name: Body
items.tip: The weight of the wine in your mouth: think skimmed milk versus whole milk versus cream.

items.name: Finish
items.tip: How long do pleasant flavors linger after swallowing or spitting?

items.name: Quality
items.tip: Use **BLIC**: Balance, Length, Intensity and Complexity. The more boxes ticked, the higher the quality.

items.name: Readiness
items.tip: Does it have the fruit, acid and tannin to improve? Or is it at its peak now?

pairings.effect: Sweet food makes wine taste **drier, more acidic, more bitter** and less fruity.
pairings.tip: Pick a wine at least as sweet as the dish: Sauternes with crème brûlée, Moscato d'Asti with fruit tarts.

pairings.effect: Umami (mushrooms, cured meat, aged cheese, soy) makes wine taste **more bitter, more acidic** and less sweet and fruity.
pairings.tip: Choose fruity, low-tannin wines, or add salt or acid to the dish.

pairings.effect: Acidic food makes wine taste **less acidic**, and fruitier and sweeter.
pairings.tip: Match high-acid dishes with high-acid wines: goat cheese with Sancerre, tomato pasta with Chianti.

pairings.effect: Salty food makes wine taste **less bitter and less acidic**, and fuller.
pairings.tip: A friendly partner: oysters with Muscadet or Chablis, salty cheese with Port.

pairings.effect: Chili makes wine taste **more bitter, more alcoholic and more acidic**, and increases the burning sensation.
pairings.tip: Choose off-dry, low-alcohol, low-tannin whites: Riesling Kabinett, Gewürztraminer.

pairings.effect: Fat and protein **soften tannin** and coat the palate.
pairings.tip: Steak with Cabernet Sauvignon or Barolo: the meat tames the wine's grip.

pairings.effect: Bitter food (radicchio, dark chocolate, grilled char) adds to the **bitterness** of tannic wines.
pairings.tip: Choose low-tannin wines with ripe fruit.

pairings.effect: Delicate dishes are overwhelmed by powerful wines, and vice versa.
pairings.tip: Match light with light (sole and Pinot Grigio) and rich with rich (lamb tagine and Châteauneuf-du-Pape).

pairings.effect: Food and wine that grew up together usually work together.
pairings.tip: Bistecca with Chianti, choucroute with Alsace Riesling, Sherry with jamón and tapas.

labels.title: Bordeaux
labels.summary: Bordeaux labels lead with the château, then the appellation. Classified growths say so.

fields.note: The estate's flagship wine (as opposed to a second wine).
**Producer.** A château is an estate with its own vineyards, castle or not.
**Classification.** One of the 61 Médoc estates ranked in 1855 (First to Fifth Growth).
**Appellation.** The more specific the place, the higher the expectations: Bordeaux → Haut-Médoc → Margaux.
Confirms the AOC (PDO). No grape names: it's a blend, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon here.
**Vintage.** Weather varies a lot in Bordeaux, so the year matters.
**Estate bottled.** Made and bottled at the property.

labels.title: Burgundy
labels.summary: In Burgundy the vineyard is king. The quality level is shown by how specific the place name is.

fields.note: **Village.** A village-level wine names the commune.
**Premier Cru + climat.** The named vineyard is a Premier Cru. A Grand Cru would show only the vineyard name, e.g. *Chambertin*.
No grape on the label: red Burgundy is Pinot Noir, white is Chardonnay.
**Vintage.**
**Producer.** *Domaine* = grower-producer. *Maison* usually means a négociant who buys grapes.

labels.title: Champagne
labels.summary: Champagne labels show the house, the style, the sweetness and a small code revealing who made it.

fields.note: **House.** Most Champagne is sold by brand.
Only sparkling wine from the Champagne region may use this word.
**Style.** Blanc de Blancs = Chardonnay only. Grand Cru = grapes from top-rated villages.
**Sweetness.** Brut Nature < Extra Brut < Brut < Extra Dry < Sec < Demi-Sec < Doux.
No year: a blend of several harvests for consistency. A vintage Champagne shows one year.
**Maker code.** NM = house buying grapes; RM = grower making their own; CM = co-operative.

labels.title: Alsace
labels.summary: Unusually for France, Alsace names the grape. Look for Grand Cru and late-harvest terms.

fields.note: **Producer.**
**Grape variety.** Alsace labels are varietal.
**Grand Cru** + vineyard name: one of 51 top sites.
**Late harvest**, usually sweet. *Sélection de Grains Nobles* = botrytized.
**Vintage.**
Tall flûte bottle is required.

labels.title: Rhône
labels.summary: Rhône labels name the appellation; the papal crossed keys mark many Châteauneuf-du-Pape bottles.

fields.note: **Producer.**
**Appellation.** A cru of the Southern Rhône: Grenache-led blends of up to 13 varieties.
'Old vines': no legal definition, but signals lower yields.
**Vintage.**

fields.text: Mis en bouteille à la propriété
fields.note: Estate bottled.

labels.title: Germany
labels.summary: German labels pack in region, village + vineyard, grape and a ripeness level (Prädikat).

fields.note: **Producer.** Weingut = wine estate.
**Region** (Anbaugebiet).
**Village + vineyard.** Wehlen (village, with -er) and Sonnenuhr (the 'sundial' vineyard).
**Grape + Prädikat.** Spätlese = late harvest ripeness; often lusciously off-dry unless *trocken*.
**Dry.** Halbtrocken/feinherb = off-dry.
**Vintage.**
Quality category and official control number.

labels.title: Italy
labels.summary: Italian labels name the place (sometimes the grape), the category (DOCG) and ageing terms.

fields.note: **Producer.** Fattoria, Tenuta, Castello = estate.
**Denomination.** The historic heart of Chianti: mostly Sangiovese.
**Top tier**: estate fruit, longest ageing. Below it: Riserva, then annata.
Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita: Italy's highest category.
**Vintage.**
Estate bottled. The black rooster neck seal marks Chianti Classico.

labels.title: Spain
labels.summary: Spanish labels show the region and an ageing category that tells you how long it rested.

fields.note: **Producer.** Bodega = winery.
**Region** (DOCa). Mostly Tempranillo.
**Ageing.** Joven → Crianza (2 yrs) → Reserva (3) → Gran Reserva (5, at least 2 in oak).
Spain's top category (DOCa / DOQ).
**Cosecha** = vintage.

labels.title: Port
labels.summary: Port labels name the shipper and the style; the style tells you how it was aged.

fields.note: **Shipper / quinta.** A quinta is a Douro estate.
**Style.** Declared only in great years, bottled after ~2 years, ages for decades. Needs decanting.
(Alternative) LBV: single year, 4–6 years in wood, ready to drink.
(Alternative) An *indication of age*: a tawny blend tasting of about 20 years.
**Vintage** (only on vintage, LBV and Colheita styles).
Fortified: about 19–22% abv.

labels.title: USA
labels.summary: New World labels lead with the brand and the grape; the AVA tells you where.

fields.note: **Brand / winery.**
**Grape.** At least 75% of the named variety (US rule).
**AVA.** At least 85% of grapes from the named AVA.
No legal meaning in the US: the producer's own top tier.
**Vintage.** At least 95% from that year when an AVA is named.
Estate = grown on land the winery owns or controls.

labels.title: Australia
labels.summary: Australian labels show brand, grape and the GI (Geographical Indication).

fields.note: **Brand.**
**Grape** (85% rule). 'Old vine' is defined by the Barossa Old Vine Charter: 35+ years.
**GI** (region).
**Vintage.**
Most Australian wines use screwcaps.
